label: Claude Sonnet 5.5
output:
Here's a draft. I kept it around 1,200 words and left out any detail about the gentleman beyond what you gave me.

---

**Last night shift**

On Saturday I did my last ever night shift. 21:00 to 07:30, majors, the same as hundreds before it. On Monday I moved onto the days-only rota, and I am not as fine about it as I thought I'd be.

I've tried to write this post three or four times since. Every draft turned into one of two things. Either it was a eulogy, which is daft, because nobody died, I just changed rotas. Or it was a rant about the NHS, and I've written enough of those. You've all read them. So this is neither. I just want to say what nights gave me and what they took, as honestly as I can.

The practical bit first. My knees aren't what they were. My sleep has been bad for years in a way I kept calling "just nights". And my GP told me, kindly but without much wiggle room, that my blood pressure is not a joke anymore. I'm 42. I've been doing this since 2012, when I did my first night as an SHO and genuinely believed I'd be sick with nerves before the end of the handover. Fourteen years is a long time to ask a body to do the opposite of what it wants.

So the move is the right one. I know it's the right one. And I'm relieved, which I'm finding hard to say out loud, because relief feels like betrayal. It feels like walking out on people who are still there at 3am and will be tonight. I don't think the relief and the guilt cancel each other out. They just sit next to each other, and I've decided to let them.

**What nights gave me**

Nights are where the department is most itself. There are fewer managers about, fewer meetings, fewer people performing. What's left is honest. People say what they mean because they're too tired to say anything else. And the kindness is real, not the polished kind. It's someone quietly taking your next patient because they can see you've hit a wall, and not mentioning it afterwards.

People think nights are about adrenaline, and I suppose some of it is. But mostly it's about staying kind at 5am when you're completely empty. That's the actual skill. Anyone can be decent at 2pm with a coffee and a full tank. The job is being patient with a frightened stranger when you've got nothing left and they need you to find something anyway. Nights taught me how to do that. I'm not sure anything else would have.

The first winter, I cried in the car park at the Infirmary because I couldn't remember whether I'd given the second dose. I sat there with the engine off, going round and round it. I had given it. Of course I had. But I remember the frost on the windscreen, and how stupid and small and alone I felt, and I think about that version of me more kindly now than I did then. He was doing fine. He just didn't know it yet.

Last winter, at about 3am, an older gentleman held my hand and told me I had his daughter's hands. I don't think he expected me to say anything back, and I didn't. I just stayed there a bit longer than the job strictly needed. He went home not long after. I won't say more than that, but I've thought about it a lot this week. It's the sort of thing that happens at night and almost never in the day, when everyone's moving too fast to be held onto. I'll miss that more than I can easily explain.

And then there's the toast. At 4am, someone always makes toast in the staff room. Nobody admits to starting it. I've asked, over the years, and got blank looks every time, like I'd accused them of something. But the smell arrives, and one by one people drift in with their eyes half shut, and for ten minutes nobody talks about anything important. Fourteen years and I still couldn't tell you who started it.

**What nights took**

Sleep, obviously. The knees. Some of my blood pressure, apparently.

And time with people I love. I missed both of my nieces' naming ceremonies. I watched them over video, because I was either on shift or flat on my back trying to recover from one. My sister, who lives in Bangalore and reads this blog, has never once complained about it. Not once. I've waited for her to, in a strange way, and she never has. If she'd been angry it would've been easier to deal with. So, Di, if you're reading this, I know. Thank you. I'm going to be better at showing up now.

I think that's the hardest thing to hold alongside the rest of it. Nights gave me some of the best of what I do and took me away from some of the people I'd do it for. Both are true. I don't have a tidy way of squaring them.

**The drive home**

On Sunday morning I drove home down the London Road. The sun was coming up, and I had the Shipping Forecast on catch-up, which is a ridiculous thing to be sentimental about but there you go. And halfway down, I realised I wouldn't see that light from that side again. Not the coming-off-shift version of it. The version where the whole world is just starting and you're the only one who's been up all night, and it feels like you're getting away with something.

I'll see the sunrise from the other side now, on the way in, with a coffee and a full night's sleep behind me. That'll be good. I'm sure it'll be good. But it's not the same light, and I wanted to say so.

**Folasade**

Our charge nurse on nights, Folasade, has done nights for twenty-two years. Twenty-two. She still beats me up the stairs. I'm sixteen years younger than I'd need to be to excuse it, and she doesn't even breathe hard. I have watched her talk to a terrified patient, redirect a doctor who was about to do something rash, settle a bay, and send a junior for a ten-minute break, all inside a quarter of an hour, and she was kinder to every one of them than she needed to be. If I know anything about staying kind at 5am, a lot of it came from watching her do it.

I think about her when I think about what's next. Not because she's leaving (she isn't), but because she's proof it can be done for a long time, by the right person, with the right amount of stubbornness. I'm not that person, and I'm okay with that now. But I'm glad I got to stand next to one.

**The toast**

So that's it. Fourteen years, one rota change, and a lot of things I'm still working out how to feel about.

Tonight, at about 4am, someone in that staff room will put bread in the toaster. They won't say anything. The smell will drift down the corridor, and a few tired people will wander in, and for ten minutes it'll be warm and quiet and nobody will be in charge of anything. I won't be there. But it'll happen. It always does, and it'll be someone else's turn to deny it.

I think that's the best thing I can say about nights. They carry on without you, and they're in good hands.

---

A few things you might change:

- I gave your sister the name "Di". That's a placeholder, so swap in her real name or cut the "Di," and keep the rest of that line.
- The "sixteen years younger than I'd need to be" line about Folasade is my invention to make the stairs joke land, and it's also a bit clumsy. Cut it if it doesn't sound like you. I don't know her age or yours relative to hers.
- If you'd rather not name a colleague, "our charge nurse" works fine, though I think the name earns its place.
